usage: The person is always marked with 를/을, never 와 'with'
The destination takes 에; here it is the speaker's own side
Adding -아 주다 turns it into a polite favor request
몰래 'secretly' is a natural adverb partner
examples: 동생 데려와.
Bring your sibling.
Bare casual command between close family
내일 친구를 파티에 데려올 거예요.
I'll bring a friend to the party tomorrow.
를 marks the person, 에 marks the destination
입양한 강아지를 보호소에서 집으로 데려왔어요.
We brought the adopted puppy home from the shelter.
Real-life adoption context; works for animals too
nuance: 데려오다 = 데리다 (to have someone in one's charge) + 오다 (to come), so it literally means 'come having someone with you' — to bring a living being TOWARD the speaker's side. The pair to learn against it is 데려가다 (take a person away from here) and 데리고 오다, which is the looser two-word version with the same meaning. The decisive split is animacy: people and animals take 데려오다/데려가다, but objects take 가져오다/가져가다 — Korean grammaticalizes 'living vs non-living' where English just says 'bring' for everything, and this is the number-one trap. Because 오다 is built in, the conjugation follows 오다: 와요/왔어요, giving 데려와요, 데려왔어요. It is neutral in register and extremely common in everyday speech: 아이를 데려오다, 친구를 데려오다.

mistakes: Saying 가방을 데려와요 for 'bring a bag' — 데려오다 is only for people/animals; an inanimate bag must be 가방을 가져와요.
Marking the person with 와/과 as in 친구와 데려와요 by copying English 'come WITH a friend' — the person is the object and takes 를/을: 친구를 데려와요.
Using 데려오다 when the movement is away from you (e.g. taking your kid to grandma's); that direction is 데려가다, not 데려오다.

usage: to take (someone) all the way home
까지 'as far as' marks the endpoint of the escort
to give (someone) a ride / drive them there
차로 with the instrumental 로 = 'by car'
-ㄹ게요 makes it a warm spontaneous offer
Near-synonym; 바래다주다 leans 'on foot, see off', 데려다주다 'deliver to a destination'
examples: 내가 데려다줄게.
I'll take you there.
Casual offer to a friend; 내가 stresses 'I'll do it'
비가 와서 집까지 데려다줄게요.
It's raining, so I'll take you home.
-아서 gives the reason; 까지 marks the endpoint
아이를 매일 아침 학교에 데려다주고 회사에 가요.
I drop my child at school every morning and then go to work.
Real routine; 데려다주고 chains to the next action
nuance: 데려다주다 stacks three pieces: 데리다 (have in charge) + -다(가) (do, then) + 주다 (give/do for someone), so it means 'escort a person to a place AND it's a favor for them'. Contrast it sharply with bare 데려가다 (take someone along), which is neutral about whose benefit it is — 데려다주다 always frames the trip as a kindness done for the passenger, exactly the nuance English 'give a ride / drop off' carries. The closest synonym 바래다주다 emphasizes accompanying/seeing off (often walking), while 데려다주다 emphasizes delivering them to the destination. For objects the parallel word is 가져다주다 (bring/fetch a thing for someone), so keep the people/thing split. Conjugation rides on 주다: 줘요/줬어요 → 데려다줘요, 데려다줬어요.

mistakes: Using 데려가다 to a friend you're kindly driving home — it loses the 'for your sake' warmth; 데려다주다 is the natural offer.
Saying 가져다주다 for a person ('데려다주다' vs '가져다주다'): 가져다주다 fetches an object, so use 데려다주다 for people.
Writing the request as 데려다 주세요 with a space and treating 주다 as separate is acceptable, but learners often drop 주다 entirely (데려다세요), which is ungrammatical — keep 주다.

usage: to go (and seek out) the teacher
A person being visited takes 를/을
to go to the office (to reach someone)
로 marks the place you head for
직접 'in person' is a very common partner adverb
to find one's way there by asking around
Fixed expression for reaching a hard-to-find place
examples: 주말에 할머니 집에 찾아가요.
I go visit grandma's place on the weekend.
Everyday visit; 에 marks the destination
문제가 있으면 직접 사무실로 찾아가세요.
If there's a problem, go to the office in person.
직접 + 로 = head there yourself to sort it out
주소만 들고 처음 가는 동네를 물어물어 찾아갔어요.
With only the address, I found my way to the unfamiliar neighborhood by asking around.
Shows the 'seek out / track down' shade
nuance: 찾아가다 = 찾다 (to look for/seek) + -아 + 가다 (to go), literally 'go seeking', so it is not plain 가다 'go' — it adds the sense of actively going TO reach a specific person or hard-to-find place, away from the speaker. Its mirror image is 찾아오다 (someone comes seeking YOU), and the direction (가 = away, 와 = toward) is the whole contrast. Beside neutral 방문하다 (Sino-Korean 訪問, 'visit', stiff/formal, used in writing and news), 찾아가다 is the warm spoken word that implies effort and intention to meet. It also has a second concrete sense: 찾아가다 = to go and collect/claim something (e.g. 택배를 찾아가다 'pick up your parcel'). It rides on 가다: 가요/갔어요 → 찾아가요, 찾아갔어요.

Substituting plain 가다 for an effortful visit and losing the 'seek out' nuance — 친구를 가요 is wrong/odd; say 친구를 찾아가요 or 친구한테 가요.
Forgetting the second meaning 'claim/pick up': students translate 택배 찾아가세요 as 'go visit the parcel'; it means 'come collect your parcel'.

usage: to grant a favor / say yes to a request
부탁 is the most frequent object of this verb
Used of parents, Santa, genies; 소원 'wish' is fixed here
to lend an ear to someone's story
Here it means listening kindly, not granting
to give in to (a child's) whining
examples: 부탁 하나만 들어줘.
Just do me one favor.
Casual; 하나만 'just one' softens the ask
제 부탁을 들어주셔서 정말 감사합니다.
Thank you so much for granting my request.
Honorific -주시- thanks a superior for saying yes
아이의 부탁을 다 들어줄 수는 없지만 오늘은 들어줬어요.
I can't grant the child's every request, but today I did.
Real situation contrasting limits and an exception
nuance: 들어주다 = 듣다 (to hear/listen) + -어 + 주다 (do for someone), and crucially the ㄷ of 듣다 turns into ㄹ before a vowel (듣 → 들-), a regular ㄷ-irregular shift, giving 들어-. The 주다 adds 'as a favour for that person', so the whole verb means either (1) accept and fulfil a request/wish, or (2) listen attentively and supportively. Contrast it with plain 듣다, which is just neutral 'hear/listen' with no benefit attached — 음악을 들어요 'I listen to music' could never be 들어줘요 unless you mean you're doing it FOR someone. Its near-synonym 들어드리다 is the same verb made humble (드리다) for elders/customers. Habitual partners: 부탁을 들어주다, 소원을 들어주다, 이야기를 들어주다. Don't confuse it with 들다 'to lift/hold', a totally different verb.

usage: Grabbing the items you need before leaving
to make sure to eat properly
챙겨 + 먹다; a super-common health/care phrase
Abstract object: take care OF something
챙기다 = not let an occasion slip by
examples: 우산 챙겨!
Grab an umbrella!
Bare casual reminder; object 우산 with no particle
나갈 때 지갑이랑 열쇠를 꼭 챙기세요.
Be sure to take your wallet and keys when you leave.
꼭 'without fail' + 챙기다 = don't forget to grab
엄마가 매일 제 도시락을 챙겨 주시고 건강도 챙겨 주세요.
Mom packs my lunch every day and looks after my health too.
Shows both senses: pack things AND care for a person
nuance: 챙기다 is one of the most useful 'caring' verbs in daily Korean, with a cluster of related senses: (1) gather/pack the things you need (짐을 챙기다), (2) make sure not to skip something, especially food (밥 챙겨 먹어 'make sure you eat'), and (3) look after a person attentively (동생 좀 챙겨 'keep an eye on your sibling'). Set it against 돌보다 (care for over time, like nursing a child or the sick): 챙기다 is quicker, more about 'making sure / not letting slip', while 돌보다 is sustained nurturing. It also contrasts with 챙겨 주다, where adding 주다 makes the care explicitly a favour for someone. The English trap is reaching for 들다 'lift' or 가지다 'have' when you mean 'grab/remember to bring' — that everyday act is 챙기다. Native warmth: 잘 챙겨 먹어요 is a standard way to say 'take care of yourself'.

usage: to walk/see (someone) all the way home
까지 marks how far you accompany them
to see (someone) off to the station
Classic endpoint for an on-foot send-off
-ㄹ까요 offers the kindness as a question
examples: 내가 정류장까지 바래다줄게.
I'll walk you to the bus stop.
Casual offer; 까지 = up to that point
밤이 늦었으니까 집까지 바래다줄게요.
It's late, so I'll see you home.
-니까 gives the reason for the offer
멀지 않으니까 바래다주지 않아도 돼요.
It's not far, so you don't have to see me off.
Politely declining with -지 않아도 돼요
nuance: 바래다주다 = 바래다 (an old verb meaning to accompany/see off) + 주다 (do as a favour), so it means walking or going along with someone partway to send them off kindly — a small act of care, warmer than just waving goodbye at the door. Compare it with its close neighbour 데려다주다: 데려다주다 stresses DELIVERING the person to a destination (often by car, you're the one in charge), whereas 바래다주다 stresses ACCOMPANYING/seeing off, traditionally on foot and out of courtesy. The dangerous look-alike is 바라다 'to wish/hope' (바라요 'I hope') and the spelling slips 바래요 — they are unrelated verbs, so keep them apart. The 주다 ending again frames the act as for the other person's benefit. Conjugation follows 주다: 바래다줘요, 바래다줬어요.

Using 데려가다 for a courteous send-off home; 데려가다 just means 'take along' — the kind 'walk you home' nuance needs 바래다주다.
Dropping 주다 and saying 바래다 alone in modern speech — on its own 바래다 is dated; the living form is 바래다주다.

usage: The respected person takes 께, the honorific of 에게
to give a New Year greeting
-(으)러 가다 = go in order to greet
examples: 사장님, 인사드리겠습니다.
Sir, allow me to greet you.
Formal self-introduction to a boss
할아버지께 새해 인사드리러 가요.
I'm going to give Grandpa a New Year's greeting.
께 honorific + -러 가다 purpose
입사 첫날이라 부서 분들께 한 분 한 분 인사드렸어요.
It was my first day, so I greeted each member of the team.
Workplace reality; humble form to all seniors
nuance: 인사드리다 is the humble (겸양) counterpart of 인사하다, built from 인사 (Sino-Korean 人事, literally 'person-affair', meaning a greeting/bow) + 드리다, the humble version of 주다 'to give'. 드리다 lowers the SPEAKER to raise the listener, so you use 인사드리다 when greeting someone older or higher in status (a teacher, boss, in-laws), whereas neutral 인사하다 is for peers and juniors. The sharp contrast is direction of respect: 인사하다 is plain, 인사드리다 humbles yourself, and there is NO 인사받다-style humble for receiving. English has no grammatical humility, so learners either over-use it with friends (sounds stiff/odd) or under-use it with elders (sounds rude). Note the natural particle is 께 ('to', honorific), not 에게/한테, when naming the respected person.

Assuming 인사 means only 'hello'; 인사 covers bows, greetings, and paying respects, so 인사드리다 can mean 'pay one's respects', not just 'say hi'.

usage: -ㄹ게요 = warm spontaneous offer to a senior
기꺼이 'gladly' is a natural polite partner
examples: 제가 도와드릴게요.
Let me help you.
Offering help to an elder/customer; 제가 = humble 'I'
짐이 무거우면 도와드릴까요?
If your bags are heavy, shall I help?
-ㄹ까요 politely offers without imposing
고객님, 무엇을 도와드릴까요?
How may I help you, sir/ma'am?
Verbatim shop/call-center phrase
nuance: 도와드리다 is the humble form of 도와주다 ('help (as a favour)'), where 돕다 (to help) becomes 도와- by the ㅂ-irregular (돕 + 아 → 도와), and the helper-benefit 주다 is upgraded to its humble twin 드리다. So it literally means 'humbly do the favour of helping' — you lower yourself to help someone above you: a customer, elder, or guest. Contrast the three levels you must keep straight: 돕다 (bare dictionary 'help'), 도와주다 (help someone, neutral/friendly), 도와드리다 (help a superior, humble). English flattens all of these to 'help', so the pitfall is using 도와주다 with a customer (too casual for service) or, conversely, 도와드리다 with a buddy (oddly stiff). The phrase 무엇을 도와드릴까요? is the fixed, must-know service line. Conjugation follows 드리다: 도와드려요, 도와드렸어요.

usage: I look forward to working with you
Set greeting when starting work or a relationship
to ask the teacher a favor
께 marks the respected person you request of
there's something I'd like to ask of you
Polite preface before making the request
to ask earnestly / please do (this for me)
꼭 좀 softens and intensifies the plea
examples: 이거 좀 부탁드려도 될까요?
May I ask you to handle this?
-아도 될까요 = polite permission-style request
바쁘시겠지만 이 일을 부탁드립니다.
I know you're busy, but I'm asking you to do this.
Honorific -시- acknowledges the senior, then requests
앞으로 잘 부탁드리겠습니다.
I look forward to your kind guidance from now on.
Standard first-day/first-meeting line at work

usage: With 친구, it means forming friendships
to date a boyfriend / be in a relationship
The classic line that starts a romantic relationship
사귄 지 + duration measures relationship length
examples: 우리 사귀자.
Let's go out.
The standard casual confession/proposal to date
새 학교에서 친구를 많이 사귀었어요.
I made lots of friends at the new school.
friendship sense; 를 marks 친구
두 사람은 사귄 지 일 년 만에 결혼했어요.

The headline trap is spelling/conjugation: the stem ends in the vowel ㅟ, which does NOT contract in standard Korean, so the polite present is 사귀어요 — never the colloquial 사겨요 you'll hear spoken but mustn't write. usage: to grow close with a friend
금방 'in no time' is a frequent partner
to want to get close (to someone)

Let's get close quickly.

I grew close to a coworker while exercising together.
-(으)면서 'while' + 와 partner particle
처음엔 어색했지만 시간이 지나니까 자연스럽게 친해졌어요.

Real arc; 친해지다 = the gradual change

So the built-in contrast is adjective vs verb: 친하다 describes the STATE of already being close (우리는 친해요 'we're close'), while 친해지다 describes the PROCESS of becoming close (우리 친해졌어요 'we've grown close'). usage: to hang out / mingle with friends
to suit well / get along well
examples: 그 옷 너한테 잘 어울려.
Those clothes really suit you.

저는 동네 친구들과 자주 어울려요.

'socialize' sense; 와 marks the people

Real situation blending 'mingle' and 'fit in'

For the social sense, compare 놀다 'to play/hang out', which is more casual and child-/leisure-flavored, whereas 어울리다 adds 'blend in, get along, fit the group' and is safe in adult/formal talk. For the matching sense, its synonym is 맞다 'to fit', but 맞다 is about correct size/fit while 어울리다 is about aesthetic harmony. English keeps 'hang out' and 'suit' in totally separate words, so the pitfall is not realizing one Korean verb does both — and that the compliment 'it suits you' is 어울려요, not 좋아 보여요. usage: to break up with a boyfriend
to say goodbye in front of the station
examples: 우리 여기서 헤어지자.

Casual; -자 = 'let's', simply splitting up to go home

와 marks the friend, 에서 the place

It is the natural antonym of 만나다 'to meet'. Keep it apart from 떠나다 'to leave (a place/person behind)', which focuses on one person departing a location, and from 헤매다 'to wander/be lost', a similar-looking but unrelated verb. The particle for the other person is 와/과 (or 하고/랑) 'with', NOT the object 를, because both sides separate mutually — a key difference from English transitive 'I left him'. usage: to take care of a child
The cared-for one takes 를/을 (it's transitive)
Adding 주다 frames the care as a favor
정성껏 'with all one's heart' is a natural partner
examples: 동생 좀 돌봐.
Look after your sibling for a bit.
Casual command; 좀 softens the request
주말에 우리 강아지 좀 돌봐 주세요.
Please look after our puppy this weekend.
돌봐 주다 = do the favor of caring; works for animals
할머니가 편찮으셔서 제가 돌봐 드리고 있어요.

The cared-for one is the direct object with 를/을.
